description: This section of our 1000+ C# multiple choice questions focuses on while loop statements in C# Programming Language.

questions.question: What will be the output of the following C# code?
questions.explanation:
j is reset to 1 each time. i % 1 is always 0, so i % j == 2 is never true and the while body never runs. The for-loop prints i and j for i = 1, 2, 3.

Output:

1 1
2 1
3 1

questions.question: What will be the output of the following C# code?
questions.explanation:
s starts at 0.1f, which is <= 0.5f, so the loop runs once. ++s adds 1, making s = 1.1f, which is then printed. 1.1f is not <= 0.5f, so the loop ends.

Output:

1.1

questions.question: What will be the output of the following C# code?
questions.explanation:
i++ < 5 tests the old value, then increments, so the body prints 1 through 5. ++i < 5 increments first, so the body prints 1 through 4. Each number is on its own line because WriteLine is used.

2
3
4
5

1
2
3
4

questions.question: What will be the output of the following C# code?
questions.explanation: The inner loop prints even values 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 and leaves x at 10. The outer loop still has x < 20, but the inner condition x < 10 is false and x is never incremented again, so the program hangs after those five numbers.

questions.question: What will be the output of the following C# code?
questions.explanation: The loop peels off remainders with n % 10 and prints each digit on its own line. For 5432 that is 2, then 3, then 4, then 5 (the digits of n from right to left). The unary plus on +r does not change the value.

questions.question: Correct syntax for while statement is:
questions.explanation: The standard form is while (condition) { }. Option a puts the condition after the block. Option d's semicolon makes an empty while, so the following block is not the loop body. Option b is syntactically valid (an extra empty statement after the block) but is not the normal while syntax.

questions.question: What will be the output of the following C# code?
questions.explanation:
The loop runs once: i++ uses 1.0f then sets i to 2.0f, and ++j sets j to 1.05f before the subtraction. 1.0f - 1.05f is a float approximation around -0.04999995. Then i is 2.0f, so i < 2.0f fails.

Output:

-0.04999995

questions.question: What will be the output of the following C# code?

options.text: infinite loop but doesn't print anything

questions.explanation: i starts at 0, so i % 10 == 0 is true and continue runs immediately. i is never incremented (the i += 10 after continue/break is unreachable), so the loop repeats forever and prints nothing. continue is valid here because it is inside a while.

questions.question: What will be the output of the following C# code?
questions.explanation:
++i increments before the test, so the body runs for i = 2 through 10 (9 times). After the failing test, i is 11. j starts at 1 and is incremented 9 times, so j is 10.

Output:

11  10
